paper_a.title: SAGA: A Fast Incremental Gradient Method (Defazio, Bach, Lacoste-Julien, 2014)

paper_b.title: Accelerating Stochastic Gradient via Predictive Variance Reduction (Johnson & Zhang, 2013)

metadata.description: SAGA extends SVRG by (1) eliminating the epoch structure (no periodic full gradient), (2) providing an unbiased gradient estimator (unlike SAG's biased one), and (3) natively supporting proximal/composite objectives. Both achieve the same O((n+kappa)*log(1/eps)) convergence rate for smooth strongly convex finite-sum problems via variance reduction. SAGA trades O(nd) storage for the gradient table in exchange for removing SVRG's epoch boundaries.

matches.explanation: Both optimize finite-sum objectives $P(w) = (1/n)\sum f_i(w)$. SAGA extends to composite objectives $P(w) = (1/n)\sum f_i(w) + h(w)$ with non-smooth proximal term $h$. SVRG considers only smooth objectives. Same core problem; SAGA's formulation is strictly more general.

The core variance reduction mechanism. Both use the same control-variate idea: subtract a stored gradient and add back its average to get an unbiased, variance-reduced estimator. SVRG: $v_t = 
abla f_{i_t}(w_t) - 
abla f_{i_t}(	ilde{w}) + 	ilde{\mu}$ where $	ilde{w}$ and $	ilde{\mu}$ are from the last epoch snapshot. SAGA: $g_k = 
abla f_j(w_k) - \phi_j^k +  ar{\phi}^k$ where $\phi_j$ is updated incrementally (not via epoch snapshot). Same mathematical structure; different mechanisms for maintaining the reference gradients.

The overall algorithm structure. SVRG has a two-loop structure (outer loop computes full gradient snapshot, inner loop runs $m$ stochastic steps). SAGA has a single loop (no epochs, no full gradient computation after initialization). SAGA additionally supports proximal steps for non-smooth regularizers. Same type of algorithm (variance-reduced SGD); different loop structure.

Both achieve the same convergence rate: $O((n + L/\mu) \log(1/\epsilon))$ for $L$-smooth, $\mu$-strongly convex finite-sum objectives. This is the optimal rate for this problem class (matching the lower bound of Woodworth & Srebro). Identical complexity guarantees.

SVRG's specific proof technique (bounding variance via smoothness and using epoch-level contraction) is different from SAGA's analysis. SAGA uses a Lyapunov function involving the gradient table errors.
SAGA's explicit comparison with SAG and SVRG, positioning itself as unifying both approaches, is a contribution of the SAGA paper. SVRG does not discuss SAGA (it predates it).
SAGA's convergence analysis for non-strongly convex objectives ($O(n/\epsilon)$ rate) is an extension not present in the original SVRG paper (which focuses on the strongly convex case).

summary: SAGA and SVRG are closely related variance-reduced stochastic gradient methods for finite-sum optimization. Both use the same control-variate idea (subtract old gradient, add back average) to reduce variance while maintaining unbiasedness. They achieve identical convergence rates: O((n + L/mu) * log(1/eps)) for smooth strongly convex problems. The key differences: (1) SVRG uses periodic full gradient snapshots (epoch structure) while SAGA maintains an incrementally updated gradient table (no epochs, at O(nd) memory cost); (2) SAGA naturally handles proximal/composite objectives while SVRG requires modifications; (3) SAGA is unbiased (correcting SAG's bias) while matching SVRG's epoch-free aspiration. SAGA explicitly positions itself as unifying SAG's incremental updates with SVRG's unbiasedness.
